title: Derandomizing black-box depth-four PIT
formal: Does there exist one deterministic uniform polynomial-time construction of hitting sets for all size-\(s\), \(n\)-variable \(\Sigma\Pi\Sigma\Pi\) arithmetic circuits, in the field-operation model specified below? Precisely, one algorithm and constants \(C>0,b\in\mathbb N\) must work for every \(n,s\ge1\), every working field \(K\), and every supplied list \(T\) of \(2s^2+1\) distinct elements of \(K\). In at most \(C(n+s+1)^b\) operations it must output a list \(H\subseteq K^n\) such that every nonzero formal polynomial computed by any allowed circuit over \(K\) has a nonzero evaluation at some point of \(H\). The algorithm receives no circuit description, coefficients, or evaluation oracle for a particular polynomial.
why: Identity testing asks whether a compact arithmetic computation represents the zero polynomial. A uniform collection of evaluations would remove randomness without inspecting the computation itself. The depth-four case is especially consequential because of its established relationship to much more general arithmetic circuits, and its unrestricted fan-ins distinguish it from several recent positive results.
status_note: The unrestricted problem is posed in the 2010 survey. The checked 2021 and 2026 primary results give restricted-family algorithms and do not cover the target’s unrestricted fan-ins and arbitrary working fields. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no general resolution. This records the scope of sources checked, not an independent certification of every later proof.

progress.text: Shpilka and Yehudayoff list the unrestricted black-box depth-four derandomization problem as Open Problem 18.
Dutta, Dwivedi and Saxena publish quasipolynomial-time black-box algorithms for two bounded-top-fan-in depth-four subclasses.
Shpilka and Tal report polynomial-size explicit hitting sets for a high-degree powering subclass with a constraint between the power and number of summands.
Garg et al. establish polynomial-time black-box testing for every fixed top fan-in with quadratic bottom factors in characteristic zero; the result appears at CCC 2026.

importance.reason: A central derandomization target in algebraic complexity. Depth four already captures a decisive barrier connected by depth reduction to general arithmetic identity testing, while black-box uniformity requires explicit evaluation sets rather than access to circuit syntax. Recent progress on restricted depth-four families leaves the unrestricted challenge substantial.

sentences: The question asks for a deterministic polynomial-time construction of evaluation points that detect every nonzero polynomial computed by a size-bounded depth-four arithmetic circuit.
The same generated set must work for every circuit of the given size without seeing its coefficients or gates.
The model charges field operations and output length, and explicitly permits a sufficiently large working field.
There is no constant bound on the top fan-in or bottom degree and no homogeneity or multilinearity assumption.
Recent polynomial-time results impose fixed fan-in, quadratic factors or powering restrictions, while the general target remains unresolved in the checked literature.

definitions: An allowed circuit is a finite directed acyclic arithmetic circuit with one output, four alternating layers of unbounded-fan-in arithmetic gates, and input leaves labeled by variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) or arbitrary constants of \(K\). From output to inputs the operations are sum, product, sum, product. Fan-in-one gates may pad smaller depth. Gates and subexpressions may be shared; the size is the total number of wires, including wires from input leaves and with repeated uses counted separately. There are at most \(s\) wires. Addition and multiplication are the only polynomial operations; division gates, exponentiation gates with compressed exponents, and tests inside the hidden circuit are excluded. In expression form the output is a sum of products of sparse polynomials, with no fixed bound on the top fan-in or on the bottom monomial degrees beyond the wire budget. The total degree is at most \(s^2\), since each bottom product has degree at most \(s\) and each upper product has at most \(s\) factors. Homogeneity, multilinearity, and bounded variable occurrence are not assumed. A nonzero polynomial means one with at least one nonzero coefficient, not merely a function that is nonzero somewhere on the original base field. The construction uses one finite program with ordinary discrete control and registers holding opaque elements of \(K\). A field addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a tested nonzero element, equality test, copy, or access to a supplied field element costs one operation; discrete control is charged by its ordinary bit operations. The only initial field values are zero, one and the entries of \(T\). Field representations carry no readable extra advice. The constants \(C,b\) are independent of characteristic, field, \(T,n,s\) and all circuit coefficients. The cost includes writing every coordinate of every output point; existence of a small set without an efficient construction does not qualify. No randomness, parameter-dependent advice, or uncharged preprocessing is allowed. The input list \(T\) makes the source’s sufficiently-large-field convention explicit. For a smaller base field \(F\), evaluations may instead take place in a supplied extension \(K\supseteq F\) with such a list; the circuit is then viewed over \(K\). Constructing or encoding that extension is outside this field-operation target. This is not a claim about bit complexity over arbitrary field presentations or an algorithm confined to evaluations inside a too-small field.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the uniform hitting-set construction and its polynomial resource bound, or prove that no such construction exists in the stated model. A positive proof must handle every allowed coefficient assignment, every working field with the supplied distinct elements, and every size and variable count. It must establish that evaluating on all of \(H\) distinguishes the zero polynomial from every nonzero polynomial in the class. A negative proof must rule out every finite uniform algorithm and polynomial bound; failure of one candidate hitting set is insufficient. A white-box algorithm, a nonconstructive existence proof, a construction with superpolynomial running time, or a construction restricted to bounded top fan-in or bottom degree does not meet this target.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 18 explicitly asks to derandomize black-box depth-four PIT. Definition 1.1 counts wires and permits unbounded fan-in at bounded depth; Remark 1.1 uses arbitrary fields by default. Section 4 permits extension-field evaluations, while Section 4.1 defines hitting sets. These conventions are made explicit in the field-operation target here.

Theorem 4.9, attributed to Agrawal and Vinay, relates polynomial-time explicit hitting sets for depth-four circuits to quasipolynomial-size explicit hitting sets for general arithmetic circuits. This is a stated consequence of solving the restricted-depth target; the card does not add a general-circuit result to the required answer.

Dutta, Dwivedi and Saxena’s 2021 Theorem 2 gives quasipolynomial-time black-box testing for bounded-top-fan-in depth-four circuits with either sums of univariates or bounded-degree bottom polynomials. Their polynomial-time theorem is white-box and for the sums-of-univariates subclass.

Garg, Oliveira, Sengupta, Shalmon and Shpilka’s 2026 Corollary 1.4 gives polynomial-time black-box PIT in characteristic zero when top fan-in is fixed and bottom degree is at most two. Its polynomial dependence is for each fixed top fan-in; it is not a polynomial-time guarantee uniform in unrestricted fan-in.

Shpilka and Tal’s February 2026 preprint gives explicit hitting sets for sums of \(r\) powers of sparse polynomials when the common power \(d\) satisfies \(d>r^2\), over characteristic zero or sufficiently large characteristic. Upper product gates in the present card may multiply unrelated factors, so the powering result covers a different restricted family.
